headline_marked: [[Ollama raises $65M Series B]] for open-source AI dev tool, now used by 8.9M developers
headline: Ollama raises $65M Series B for open-source AI dev tool, now used by 8.9M developers
summary: The popular open-source AI tool helps developers run open-weight models on their PCs and offers cloud services, now serving 8.9 million monthly users.
details: Ollama, the popular open-source AI tool, has successfully raised a $65 million Series B funding round led by Theory Ventures. This latest investment brings the company's total funding to $88 million, following a previous $15 million Series A.

Launched in 2023, Ollama enables developers to run open-weight AI models directly on their personal computers, making setup quick and easy. The tool has gained significant traction, boasting 176,000 stars and nearly 17,000 forks on GitHub.

Beyond local execution, Ollama also provides cloud services, allowing developers to access larger, more complex models through various subscription tiers, ranging from free to $100 per month. Its usage tracking is based on GPU time rather than token limits, offering a different approach to resource management.

Founders Jeff Morgan and Michael Chiang previously built Docker Desktop, a tool that simplified cloud application deployment. They aim to replicate this success for AI, abstracting away hardware complexities to make AI model deployment more accessible.

Morgan stated that open models were initially difficult for programmers to use, leading to Ollama's creation. Now, the platform is utilized by over 8.9 million developers monthly, including users in 85% of Fortune 500 companies, all managed by a lean team of just 14 employees.

The rise of open-weight models capable of agentic tasks like coding has driven increased interest from enterprises and AI startups. Many are turning to more affordable open models to manage high inference expenses, reserving closed models for specific needs.

While some users initially criticized Ollama's cloud business as a distraction from its free project, the company views it as an extension of its mission. The cloud service helps developers access state-of-the-art models that are too large to run on individual computers, ensuring continued utility and growth.

headline_marked: [[AMD Zen 6 Medusa Point 10-core APU]] faster than Ryzen AI 9 HX 370 & Ryzen AI Max+ 395
headline: AMD Zen 6 Medusa Point 10-core APU faster than Ryzen AI 9 HX 370 & Ryzen AI Max+ 395
summary: A leaked AMD Zen 6 "Medusa Point" APU scored 22% higher in single-core than the Ryzen AI 9 HX 370 and even beat the Ryzen AI 9 Max+ 395 in single-core benchmarks, hinting at significant next-gen performance.
details: AMD's next-gen mobile CPUs, codenamed "Medusa Point" and based on the Zen 6 microarchitecture, have begun to leak ahead of their expected CES 2027 announcement. A 10-core SKU recently appeared on Geekbench, showing impressive early performance.

The engineering sample, identified as "AMD Eng Sample 100-000001713-33_N" under the "AMD Plum-MDS1" platform, is a 10-core (4+6) chip with 20 threads. It's clocked at approximately 2.0 GHz, featuring 10MB of L2 cache and 32MB of L3 cache, likely a purported Ryzen AI 9 565.

In Geekbench, the chip scored 3,174 points in single-core and 15,092 points in multi-core. These results surpass the Strix Point flagship APU, the Ryzen AI 9 HX 370, by an average of 22% in single-core and 13% in multi-core performance.

The Medusa Point APU also outperformed the Strix Halo flagship, the Ryzen AI 9 Max+ 395, by over 400 points in single-core, though it lagged in multi-core. This new listing is also significantly better than a prior 10-core Medusa Point leak.

While these early benchmarks suggest a noticeable performance leap from Zen 6 architectural improvements, it's crucial to remember this is an engineering sample. Medusa Point is still months away, and final performance may vary.
